name: Chloe Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the front desk at the housing benefit office on Station Road, so my day starts with the queue at half eight. People come in with eviction letters, rent arrears, a landlord who won't sign a form, and I take the details down and open the case. I'm still slow on the system, honestly, and my supervisor Grace checks most of what I send through. The part I like is when someone walks out knowing they'll keep their flat.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The screens, mostly. We've got three different systems that don't talk to each other, and every few months there's a new 'digital first' push from head office. I write my notes on paper first and type them up after, which drives Grace mad. My partner Tomasz is a nurse, and some nights we just sit there too tired to cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like the last five years, to be fair. Head office keeps promising some smart tool will fix the backlog, and it never does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the union group chat. We've had chatbots on the council website for two years and people still queue at my desk because the bot couldn't understand a rent arrears letter. I'd say the money should go on staff, not software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my job and keep being a bit behind. The routine bits it might take are the copy-and-paste jobs I hate, so fine. But they'd use any time saved to give us more cases each, not to give claimants longer at the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd finally go on the system training I keep putting off, because I need to get faster whatever happens. I'd keep paying into my savings like now, and keep going to the union branch meeting once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. My savings are solid, the flat my nan left me brings in rent, and there are other benefit offices across the city if this one gets grim. It's tiring, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said any time saved would turn into more cases. What would that look like on a normal week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I carry about forty open cases. If the tool shaves ten minutes off each form, someone upstairs does the sum and I'm on fifty by spring. Nobody ever turns saved time into a longer chat with a frightened tenant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the office would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, actually. She's been there nineteen years and she does everything the long way because she knows where the system lies. If they bring in a tool that does her checking, I think they'd push her out first. She's the reason I'm learning at all.

say: The **chatbot hype** never cleared a single queue at my desk.
Put the money into **more caseworkers**, not another software contract.
think: My **job is safe**, but any saved time becomes bigger **caseloads**.
I still need to get **faster on the system**, whatever happens with AI.
do: **Book the system training** I've put off since the spring.
Keep **saving monthly** and keep letting my nan's flat.
Go to the **union branch meeting** every month as I do now.
feel: **Tired** of the churn, but **calm** about my own job and money.
S0.quote: We've had chatbots on the council website for two years and people still queue at my desk because the bot couldn't understand a rent arrears letter.
fieldNote: She trusts **paper notes** and people over screens, and treats AI as another head-office fad.
Her **inherited flat** and savings give her real security, and she knows it.
Her worry here is **caseload creep** and her supervisor, not losing her own job.

steps.text: Book the housing benefit system training before the new year
Attend the monthly union branch meeting at the town hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I can actually see happening. Writing, checking, answering people: that's my whole job description, read back to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it out loud at the branch meeting: if a machine is going to make decisions about people's homes, a human signs it off, full stop. Online I'd share every story where the software got someone's rent wrong. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the obvious one to go. I'm junior, I'm slow, and I'm the person who won't touch the new tools. When they stop replacing leavers, the next restructure looks at people like me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and fight it through the union first, because that's what the union is for. I'd also start looking at jobs where you sit with people, like the tenancy support team at the housing charity on Mill Lane. And I'd stop spending on holidays this year and put that into savings, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not the end of the world, because I've got money behind me and Tomasz's job isn't going anywhere. But it's the feeling of being the slow kid who gets left behind, again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the tenancy support job. What makes it different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tenancy support job is mostly visits and phone calls, sitting in someone's kitchen sorting out their letters. It pays a bit less than the council. But a program can't knock on a door and see that the fridge is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're worried about being the one who won't touch the tools. Would you start using them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I still won't. Maybe that's stubborn. I've seen the tool on the housing system suggest a claimant's income from an old payslip, and Grace caught it, and the family would've lost three hundred a month. I don't want to be the one who clicks yes on that.

say: A **human must sign off** every decision about someone's home.
I'd share every story where **software got rent wrong**.
think: I'm junior, slow and **refuse the tools**, so I'm first in line.
When they **stop replacing leavers**, people like me get looked at first.
do: **Raise human sign-off** at the union branch meeting this winter.
Apply for **tenancy support work** at the Mill Lane housing charity.
**Skip this year's holiday** and put that money into savings.
feel: **Anxious**, and left behind like **the slow kid** again.
Steadied by savings and a **partner's secure job**.
S1.quote: A program can't knock on a door and see that the fridge is empty.
fieldNote: She sees her own job description in the card and **names herself** as the first to go.
Her refusal of the tools rests on a **real error** her supervisor caught.
She'd rather **move to face-to-face** work than learn the software.

steps.text: Push for human sign-off on housing decisions at the union branch
Apply for tenancy support work at the Mill Lane housing charity
Skip this year's holiday and bank the money instead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not even long enough to finish my probation reviews properly. Everything I do is at a screen, so the whole thing lands on me at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not weather. Someone in government decides to let a machine run benefits, and someone signs the contract. I'd be at every protest outside the council and I'd be pushing the union for a no-redundancy deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my desk is gone by 2029. Even Grace's desk is gone. A machine that's better than a person at reading forms doesn't need a junior who types up paper notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd look at hands-on work, because the robots come three years later. I've thought about training as a support worker in a care home, like the ones Tomasz deals with on the wards. I'd keep the savings untouched and the flat let, so we've got something if both our jobs wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it. I'd be up at night working out how long the savings last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would your savings carry you, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two years if I'm careful, longer with the rent from the flat. So I'm not on the street. But two years of savings isn't a career, it's a waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care work would also meet robots around 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work gets me to maybe 2031, and then the robots come for lifting and washing too. I know that. But I'd rather have three years doing something real with my hands than sit at a desk waiting to be switched off.

say: Letting machines run benefits is **a political choice**, not weather.
I'd be at **every protest** and pushing for a **no-redundancy deal**.
think: My desk is **gone by 2029**, and my supervisor's too.
**Two years of savings** is a waiting room, not a career.
do: **Start care-worker training** for hands-on work before 2029.
**Leave the savings untouched** and keep my nan's flat let.
**Join protests** outside the council and push the union hard.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a dropping stomach and **sleepless sums** at night.
S2.quote: Two years of savings isn't a career, it's a waiting room.
fieldNote: Her answer to fast AGI is **politics and protest** first, then hands-on work.
She counts on the **three-year robot gap** knowing it only delays things.
Savings and the **rental flat** stop panic but not alarm.

steps.text: Join union protests outside the council against benefit automation
Start a care-worker course at the college in the new year
Leave the savings untouched and keep the flat let

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more than two, but I'm still at a screen all day. It just means I watch it coming instead of getting hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to set rules, so let's set them. Things like a human caseworker for anyone at risk of losing their home, written into law. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, and I'd vote for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for me to get out with my dignity. It's not enough for the job to survive. I'd rather leave on my own terms than be the last caseworker at the benefit office with the lights going off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stay at the council and do the tenancy support job's evening course, so I'm qualified for face-to-face work. By year three I'd move across, and I'd keep the savings for the gap. Tomasz and I would put off buying a bigger place until we know what's left standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, if I'm honest. Less panicky than two years, but I know where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned holding off on a bigger place. What were you planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a house near his hospital next year. Now I'd say wait. Rent's annoying, but a mortgage on two jobs that might shrink is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that the union would have time to win something. With two years, they'd be fighting a fire. With five, we could actually get a law about human caseworkers through.

say: We have **time to set rules**, so set them now.
Anyone at risk of losing a home should get a **human caseworker by law**.
think: Five years lets me **leave with dignity**, but the job won't survive.
I'd rather go on **my own terms** than be the last one there.
do: Take the **tenancy support course** in the first year.
**Move to face-to-face work** by the third year.
**Delay buying a house** with my partner near the hospital.
feel: **Alarmed**, though **less panicky** than with two years.
S3.quote: I'd rather leave on my own terms than be the last caseworker at the benefit office with the lights going off.
fieldNote: Extra time lets her **plan an exit** rather than just fight.
She ties the timing to how much the **union can win**.
She puts off a **house purchase** on purpose, despite her savings.

steps.text: Take the tenancy support evening course at the city college
Vote for parties promising human caseworkers for housing cases
Delay buying a house near the hospital with my partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other career's worth of time, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same ending, so the same fight: people deciding about people. But I'd sound less angry. I'd say we've got a decade to make sure benefits offices still have someone at the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can be stubborn for a bit longer. I'd still be at the council for a few years. But I'd know I'm not retiring from that desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am for now and get properly good at the casework, without the AI bits. In about year three I'd start a social work degree part-time, because social workers sit with families in their kitchens, and that's much harder for a computer to replace than my typing. The savings would pay for the course without touching the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slow anxious. Like knowing the rent goes up next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools at work in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because they'd make us. Probably I'd learn the bare minimum to keep my seat. But I wouldn't build a career on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does starting a degree at thirty-something worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty-seven and newly qualified is fine. Tomasz qualified at thirty-one. And honestly I'd be a better social worker after ten years of hearing people's stories on Station Road.

say: Same ending, **same fight**: people deciding about people.
We have **a decade** to keep someone at every benefits desk.
think: I can stay **stubborn a bit longer**, but I won't retire from that desk.
Ten years is enough for a **whole second career**.
do: **Get properly good** at casework over the next few years.
Start a part-time **social work degree** around year three.
Pay the **fees from savings** without touching the flat.
feel: **Slow anxiety**, like knowing the **rent rises** next year.
S4.quote: Social workers sit with families in their kitchens, and that's much harder for a computer to replace than my typing.
fieldNote: Time lets her **choose social work**, a people-facing route she trusts.
She would learn **the bare minimum** of AI and no more.
Her tone softens, but her **core belief** in human judgement holds.

steps.text: Start a part-time social work degree around the third year
Pay the course fees from savings, not the flat
Keep working the housing desk without using AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Two years is no time to retrain and everything I do is at a screen. What would help is a promise in law that people facing eviction still get a human caseworker, and free retraining for council staff into face-to-face jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the claimants. Everyone talks about us losing our jobs, but the people at my desk can't use the website now. If it all goes to machines, I worry most about the old man who brings his letters in a carrier bag.

headlineQuote: If it all goes to machines, I worry most about the old man who brings his letters in a carrier bag.
portrait: A **27-year-old housing benefit caseworker** on a city front desk, junior and still slow on the systems.
She writes **paper notes first**, never uses AI, and trusts her long-serving supervisor's checking.
Strong savings and an **inherited flat** keep her calm in the plateau but not beyond.
She answers fast change with **union action and protest**, then a move to face-to-face work.
With ten years, she'd fund a **social work degree** from savings and stay people-focused.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain from a screen job.
whatWouldHelp: A legal right to a **human caseworker** for anyone facing eviction.
**Free retraining** for council staff into face-to-face jobs.
